title: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
summary: Why VPNs, firewalls and gateways became a favourite way in, five real appliance breaches at advisory level, and how to inventory, prioritise, watch, rebuild and retire what you expose.
outcomes: Explain why internet-facing appliances became a leading way in, using KEV, Mandiant and NCSC evidence
Describe the bug class behind the Pulse, FortiOS, Citrix Bleed, Ivanti and PAN-OS breaches, and why each fix works
Explain why patching an exploited appliance does not evict an intruder or revoke stolen passwords and sessions
Run exposure management: outside-in discovery, inventory with owners, and a KEV watch list for edge products
Apply BOD 26-04 deadlines and BOD 23-02 management interface rules to real cases
Detect appliance compromise from outside the box with forwarded logs, session anomalies and outbound traffic
Respond to a compromised appliance: preserve evidence, rebuild, rotate every secret it held, and hunt
Decide when to harden, replace or retire an edge device, including end-of-support devices under BOD 26-02

lessons.title: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first

blocks.md:
Ana works from home. Ana's laptop connects to `vpn.example.com`, the company's VPN gateway (recall from *How networks work*: a VPN, virtual private network, carries private traffic through an encrypted tunnel across a public network). Before Ana has typed a password, the gateway has already accepted the laptop's TCP connection, finished a TLS handshake and parsed its first HTTP request.

So has every other machine on the internet that connects to it. That one fact explains most of this course: the gateway runs code for strangers, and it sits on the line between outside and inside.

An **edge device** is, in the words of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS, Canada's national cyber security agency), a network hardware or software component that bridges "internally managed networks and external, untrusted networks such as the internet". The US government's binding directive on old edge devices (BOD 26-02, lesson 12) lists load balancers, firewalls, routers, switches, wireless access points and network security appliances.

The families you meet in this course:

- **SSL VPN gateways**: VPNs that run over TLS (named after SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, the protocol TLS replaced), so they work through a browser on port 443.
- **Firewalls**, including next-generation firewalls (recall from *Network attacks and defences*), which often include an SSL VPN.
- **ADCs** (application delivery controllers): load balancers that also terminate TLS and log users in.
- **Gateways** for email and file transfer.

Most of these are **appliances**: sealed products, hardware or a virtual machine image, running the vendor's own operating system. You configure them through the vendor's menus but cannot install your own software on them or read every file.

Why attackers aim here was put plainly in a February 2024 blog post by Dave Chismon of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), [Products on your perimeter considered harmful (until proven otherwise)](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/products-on-your-perimeter). Client software such as browsers and Office has had "a decade of being put through the fire", so phishing a laptop got harder. Attackers turned to "products on the network perimeter (such as file transfer applications, firewalls and VPNs)", where many bugs "are well-understood classes of web vulnerability", and where products "typically don't have decent logging".

blocks.title: Where an edge appliance sits, and what it can reach

nodes.label:
SOC: EDR agents on
laptops and servers

scenes.caption: Every request from outside meets the appliance first, from Ana and from strangers alike. The code that parses requests before login is the appliance's pre-authentication attack surface.

After Ana logs in, the appliance checks the password against Active Directory (the Windows directory of company accounts) and forwards Ana inside. It holds a service account and sees each password typed into it.
Take over the appliance and you inherit its position: reach inside plus credentials. In one case CISA found Volt Typhoon used a domain admin account stored on an unpatched FortiGate firewall.
The SOC (security operations centre) watches laptops and servers with EDR agents. The appliance runs no agent, so what happens on it is invisible unless its logs leave the box.

blocks.md:
Two terms from that figure. **EDR** (endpoint detection and response) is an agent installed on each computer that records processes, files and network connections and can stop suspicious ones. Mandiant (Google Cloud's incident response firm, more below) notes in its M-Trends 2026 report that espionage groups "deliberately target edge and core network devices, such as virtual private networks (VPNs) and routers, that typically lack standard endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry".

**MFA** (multi-factor authentication) asks for a second proof besides the password, such as a code from a phone app.

**Volt Typhoon** is the name US agencies use for a People's Republic of China state-sponsored group. Advisory AA24-038A from CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, February 2024) describes how it "likely obtained initial access by exploiting CVE-2022-42475 in a network perimeter FortiGate 300D firewall that was not patched", then "compromised a domain admin account stored inappropriately on the device".

**How big is the problem?** Mandiant publishes M-Trends every year from its investigations. In [M-Trends 2026](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/m-trends-2026), exploits were the most common initial infection vector "for the sixth consecutive year, accounting for 32% of intrusions" in 2025 (33% in 2024). Verizon's 2026 [Data Breach Investigations Report](https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/dbir/) (DBIR) found that 31% of breaches now start with exploited software vulnerabilities, overtaking stolen passwords as the top way in.

A **zero-day** is a vulnerability exploited before a patch exists; an **n-day** is one first exploited after the patch is out (Mandiant's definitions).

You can measure part of this yourself. KEV (recall from *Security from zero*: CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue) is published as JSON. The script counts entries for seven edge product lines.

blocks.code:
import json, urllib.request
URL = "https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json"
kev = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(URL, headers={"User-Agent": "kev-demo"})))

# (label, vendor, words that must appear in the product name)
LINES = [
    ("Ivanti/Pulse Connect Secure", ("Ivanti", "Pulse Secure"), ("Connect Secure",)),
    ("Cisco ASA / FTD",             ("Cisco",),   ("Adaptive Security", "Firepower")),
    ("Fortinet FortiOS/FortiProxy", ("Fortinet",), ("FortiOS", "FortiProxy")),
    ("Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway",("Citrix",),  ("NetScaler", "Application Delivery")),
    ("Palo Alto PAN-OS",            ("Palo Alto Networks",), ("PAN-OS",)),
    ("SonicWall SMA/SonicOS",       ("SonicWall",), ("SMA", "SonicOS", "Remote Access")),
    ("F5 BIG-IP",                   ("F5",),      ("BIG-IP",)),
]
print("KEV catalog", kev["catalogVersion"], "entries:", kev["count"])
for label, vendors, words in LINES:
    hits = [v for v in kev["vulnerabilities"]
            if v["vendorProject"] in vendors and any(w in v["product"] for w in words)]
    ransom = sum(v["knownRansomwareCampaignUse"] == "Known" for v in hits)
    print(f"{label:29} {len(hits):3}  ransomware-linked: {ransom}")
blocks.caption: Runs as is with Python 3 and internet access. It matches vendor names exactly and product names by keyword, a simple rule you can tighten.

scenes.caption: All KEV entries per product line: each is a vulnerability CISA has reliable evidence was exploited in the wild.
Entries KEV marks as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. FortiOS: 12 of 15. Edge bugs are not only a nation-state problem; criminals use them to get in too.

blocks.md: A common misconception: "it is a security product, so it is secure". Firewalls and VPNs are software written under the same pressures as any other, and they run on the most exposed spot you have. KEV counts measure exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how widely a product is deployed; they are not a ranking of code quality.

An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

blocks.question: Why is a VPN gateway often a more valuable target than an employee laptop?
options: It usually has a faster processor
Laptops cannot be attacked over the network
VPN traffic is not encrypted
Anyone can reach it before login, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it usually runs no EDR
blocks.explain: The three properties together: pre-authentication exposure, a privileged position (passwords, service accounts, routes inside) and little monitoring. A laptop typically has EDR and must first be reached through phishing.

blocks.question: FortiOS/FortiProxy has 15 KEV entries (12 ransomware-linked); F5 BIG-IP has 8. What can you conclude from these counts alone?
options: BIG-IP is about twice as secure as FortiOS
FortiOS should be banned
Little about code quality: KEV records exploitation that was found and reported, which also depends on how common and attractive a product is
KEV only covers network products
blocks.explain: KEV is evidence of exploitation in the wild, not a defect rate. Deployment size, attacker interest and who investigates all affect the count. Use it to decide what to watch and patch fastest, not to grade vendors on its own.

lessons.title: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust

blocks.md:
Compare two machines. On a Linux web server you run, you can install an EDR agent, read any file, keep logs for a year and update one package at a time. On a VPN appliance you usually get a vendor web console and a restricted command line. You cannot add an agent. An update replaces the whole **firmware** (here: the complete operating system image the vendor ships for the device) and needs a reboot. The appliance keeps a small log on its own disk.

Each difference opens a gap. This lesson names three: the patch gap, the telemetry gap and the trust gap.

**The patch gap.** Rebooting the VPN disconnects everyone working remotely, so upgrades wait for a change window. When Fortinet reported in September 2021 that credentials for 87,000 FortiGate SSL VPN devices had been leaked from devices still unpatched against a May 2019 bug (lesson 3), it listed reasons customers defer patching: "the inability to take critical systems offline", "onerous testing requirements for new updates" and "understaffed or inexperienced security teams".

Sometimes there is no patch to apply. Ivanti's January 2024 zero-days had only a temporary mitigation for three weeks (lesson 5), and old devices past their support date get no patches at all (lesson 12).

**The telemetry gap.** Telemetry is the stream of logs and measurements a system produces about itself. Mandiant's Citrix Bleed investigation (lesson 4) found that NetScaler's web server "does not record requests (or errors) to the vulnerable endpoint", and that the default log rotation keeps "25 files per log type (e.g., ns.log) and 100 Kilobytes per log, therefore recording 2.5 megabytes in total". In most cases that "will not have enough space to cover the full period of an investigation".

The script turns 2.5 MB into hours of history. The line size is an assumption; change it to match your logs.

blocks.code:
# NetScaler default log rotation, per Mandiant: 25 files x 100 KB = 2.5 MB
capacity = 25 * 100_000                        # bytes kept on the box
line = 300                                     # assumed bytes per log line
for per_sec in (0.1, 1, 5, 20):
    hours = capacity / (per_sec * line) / 3600
    print(f"{per_sec:5} lines/s: oldest line is {hours:6.2f} hours old")

# output
  0.1 lines/s: oldest line is  23.15 hours old
    1 lines/s: oldest line is   2.31 hours old
    5 lines/s: oldest line is   0.46 hours old
   20 lines/s: oldest line is   0.12 hours old
blocks.caption: Busy gateways write many lines per second, so the on-box history can be shorter than a lunch break. Only logs forwarded off the box survive.

blocks.title: Hours of history a 2.5 MB on-box log holds

scenes.caption: At 300 bytes per line, 1 line per second fills 2.5 MB in about 2.3 hours. Every tenfold rise in traffic cuts the history tenfold.

At 1 line per second or more, even a hundred times more local space gives days, not months. Attackers stay far longer: M-Trends 2026 reports BRICKSTORM backdoors on appliances with dwell times of nearly 400 days.

blocks.md: Worse, a capable intruder can erase what little there is. When the security firm Volexity examined a hacked Ivanti VPN in December 2023, it found "its logs had been wiped and logging had been disabled". M-Trends 2026 advises forwarding "critical network device logs" to central storage and keeping them "well beyond standard 90-day windows". That central store is usually a **SIEM** (security information and event management system: a server that collects, keeps and searches logs from many sources), fed by **syslog**, the standard protocol network devices use to send log lines to another machine.

**The trust gap.** Appliances are trusted with secrets. CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) showed in advisory AA20-107A that a Pulse Secure file-read bug leaked "plaintext Active Directory credentials" and even the password of the domain administrator used to join the device to the domain. In AA24-060B it found Ivanti appliances could reveal "domain administrator cleartext credentials, if saved" during setup.

You also cannot easily check what code the appliance runs: the vendor's image is closed, often encrypted, and any integrity tool runs on the box it is checking (lesson 5).
Treat an appliance as a server you cannot see into. Get its logs out as they are written, limit the secrets it holds, and plan in advance for the day you must rebuild it.

blocks.question: A NetScaler writes about 5 lines per second of roughly 300 bytes, with the default 2.5 MB of local logs, and nothing is forwarded. Investigators arrive the next morning. What history is on the box?
options: About the last half hour; older lines have rotated away
The last 90 days
Everything since the last reboot
Nothing; NetScaler does not log at all
blocks.explain: 2,500,000 / (5 x 300) is about 1,667 seconds, roughly 28 minutes. Without forwarding to a SIEM, the night's activity is gone. Mandiant warned exactly this for Citrix Bleed investigations.

blocks.question: Which feature from the NCSC forensic guidance most directly lets you notice that an appliance's configuration was changed while its own logs were wiped?
options: A larger local disk
Disabling time synchronisation
A web console in more languages
A heartbeat sent off the box that carries a SHA256 digest of the current configuration
blocks.explain: The digest leaves the device regularly, so a change shows up in the SIEM even if the device's local log is later cleared. A larger disk still lives on the box the intruder controls.

lessons.title: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords

blocks.md:
A web server maps the path in a URL to a file under one folder, its **web root**. In a path, `..` means "the parent folder". **Path traversal** is the bug where the server joins the request's path onto the web root without checking where the result ends up, so a path full of `..` climbs out and reads any file the server process can read.

MITRE's CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration, a catalogue of software weakness types) calls it CWE-22, "Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory". Both bugs in this lesson are CWE-22 in KEV, and both were in SSL VPNs.

**The research.** In 2019 Orange Tsai and Meh Chang of the DEVCORE Security Research Team reported pre-authentication bugs in several leading SSL VPNs and presented them at the Black Hat USA conference on 8 August 2019.

**FortiOS** (the operating system of Fortinet's FortiGate firewalls). Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-18-384, published 24 May 2019, describes CVE-2018-13379: "a path traversal vulnerability in the FortiOS SSL VPN web portal may allow an unauthenticated attacker to download FortiOS system files". Affected: 5.4.6 to 5.4.12, 5.6.3 to 5.6.7 and 6.0.0 to 6.0.4, only with SSL VPN enabled; fixed in 5.4.13, 5.6.8, 6.0.5 and 6.2.0. The only workaround was to turn the SSL VPN off. The advisory warns that exploit code "to obtain the credentials of logged in SSL VPN users was disclosed", and that two-factor authentication stops stolen passwords from being enough.

**Pulse Connect Secure** (Pulse Secure's SSL VPN, known today as Ivanti Connect Secure). Pulse Secure published advisory SA44101 with fixes on 24 April 2019 for CVE-2019-11510, a pre-authentication arbitrary file read. CISA's explanation of the root cause is one sentence: "directory traversal is hard coded to be allowed if the path contains" one particular folder used for HTML5 remote access. Requesting a cache file through it could "leak plaintext credentials of enterprise users".

The toy server below has the same shape of mistake: a `..` rule with an exception based on what the raw text contains. Paths and files are made up.

blocks.code:
import posixpath

ROOT = "/opt/portal/web"
OPEN_DIR = "/assets/html5/"          # files anyone may fetch before login

def vulnerable(path):
    # Rule: refuse "..", except under the open assets folder (it needs it).
    if ".." in path and OPEN_DIR not in path:
        return "403 refused"
    return "200 serves " + posixpath.normpath(ROOT + path)

def fixed(path):
    # Normalise first, then check where the path really points.
    full = posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join(ROOT, path.lstrip("/")))
    if not full.startswith(ROOT + "/"):
        return "403 refused"
    return "200 serves " + full

tests = ["/assets/html5/app.js",
         "/../../../etc/passwd",
         "/assets/html5/../../../../data/sessions.db"]
for t in tests:
    print(t)
    print("  vulnerable:", vulnerable(t))
    print("  fixed:     ", fixed(t))

# output
/assets/html5/app.js
  vulnerable: 200 serves /opt/portal/web/assets/html5/app.js
  fixed:      200 serves /opt/portal/web/assets/html5/app.js
/../../../etc/passwd
  vulnerable: 403 refused
  fixed:      403 refused
/assets/html5/../../../../data/sessions.db
  vulnerable: 200 serves /opt/data/sessions.db
  fixed:      403 refused
blocks.caption: Vulnerable and fixed checks side by side. The fix normalises the path first, then tests where it really points. Real servers should also resolve symbolic links (os.path.realpath) before the test.

blocks.title: One request through both checks

scenes.caption: The request contains '..', which should be refused. But it also contains the open folder's name.
The exception fires: '..' is present, but so is OPEN_DIR, so the condition is false and no refusal happens.
Only now is the path resolved, and it lands outside the web root: the session database is served.
The fixed check resolves first. The four '..' climb past /opt/portal/web, so the result no longer starts with the root.
Refused. The test is on where the path ends up, not on what text it contains, so no spelling of the path can get around it.

blocks.md:
**Why string rules fail.** A check on the raw text has to predict every way to spell a path: exceptions, URL encoding, doubled slashes. Normalising first and comparing the final location removes the guessing. Better still, do not build file paths from user input at all: map request names to files through a fixed list.

**What happened next.** By 24 August 2019, researchers at Bad Packets counted over 14,500 Pulse servers still unpatched. In January 2020 CISA warned of continued exploitation, noting media reports of criminals installing REvil ransomware through unpatched Pulse servers. In April 2020 CISA added the twist this lesson is about.

blocks.title: Stolen before the patch, used after it (CISA AA20-107A)

scenes.caption: Before the patch: one unauthenticated file read returns a cache holding users' plaintext Active Directory passwords.
The admin applies the April 2019 fix. The hole is closed, and the scanner now reports the device as clean.
Months later the attacker logs in with a real user's password, from Tor (an anonymising network) or a rented server. The VPN asks Active Directory, which says yes.
Inside, the attacker moves with remote services and stolen accounts. CISA: EDR "did not detect this type of activity because the threat actors used legitimate credentials and remote services".

blocks.md:
CISA's alert AA20-107A (April 2020) reported incidents "where compromised Active Directory credentials were used months after the victim organization patched their VPN appliance". In one case an actor tried to sell the credentials after failing to deploy ransomware; CISA had seen the same actor drop ransomware at hospitals and US government entities.

FortiOS followed the same path. In November 2020 Fortinet wrote that over 18 months after the advisory, "a large number of devices" were still unpatched and their IP addresses were reportedly being sold. On 8 September 2021 it reported that an actor had published "SSL-VPN access information to 87,000 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices", adding that devices patched since remained at risk "if the passwords were not reset". Both CVEs entered KEV on 3 November 2021, the day the catalogue was created.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: patch internet-facing VPNs within days of an advisory; require MFA on VPN logins, which Fortinet named as the mitigation for stolen passwords.
- *Detect*: CISA told Pulse owners to turn on logging of unauthenticated requests (and forward it, since it can overwrite local logs), search for traversal sequences in requested paths, review sessions from unexpected locations, and run its free IOC (indicator of compromise) scanner. A network IDS that sees the VPN's outside interface can also flag traversal requests.
- *Respond*: if exploitation is possible, change the passwords of all Active Directory accounts, including administrators and service accounts (CISA's advice, since the device could leak even the domain administrator's password), and look for new scheduled tasks and remote-access tools on internal hosts.
Patching closes the hole. It does not un-leak what already leaked. After any file-read bug on an edge device, rotate every secret the device held and every password typed through it.

blocks.question: In the toy server, why is '/assets/html5/../../../../data/sessions.db' served by the vulnerable check?
options: Python's normpath has a bug
The file is inside the web root
The rule tests the raw text for an allowed folder name, and only resolves the path after deciding
The '..' characters are removed automatically
blocks.explain: The decision is made on the text, which contains OPEN_DIR, so the '..' refusal is skipped. The fixed version decides on the resolved location, which is outside the root.

blocks.question: An organisation patched its Pulse appliance in May 2019 and saw no alerts afterwards. In 2020 an attacker logs in through it as a real employee. What was missing?
options: A second firmware upgrade
Resetting every password that could have been read from the appliance before the patch, and requiring MFA
A reboot after patching
A stronger TLS cipher
blocks.explain: The patch stopped new file reads. Passwords already copied stayed valid until changed, and without MFA a password alone was enough to log in. This is exactly CISA's AA20-107A finding.

lessons.title: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions

blocks.md:
When you log in to a website, the server gives your browser a **session cookie**: a long random token it stores next to your identity (recall cookies from *How networks work*). Every later request carries the cookie, and whoever presents it is treated as you. If the login included **MFA** (multi-factor authentication: a second proof besides the password, such as a code from a phone app), the cookie is only issued after both checks.

So a stolen cookie skips the password and the MFA. Citrix Bleed handed attackers other people's cookies through a **buffer over-read**: a program sends more bytes than it filled, so whatever lies next in memory leaks out with the reply.

**The facts.** NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway are application delivery and remote access appliances from Cloud Software Group, the parent of NetScaler and Citrix. On 10 October 2023 it released fixed builds for CVE-2023-4966, a "sensitive information disclosure" found by its own team, with no known exploitation at the time. Only appliances set up as a gateway (for example a VPN virtual server or RDP proxy) or as an AAA virtual server were affected (AAA: authentication, authorization and accounting). Its score: CVSS 9.4. There was no workaround, and signatures for web application firewalls (WAFs, filters for HTTP requests) could not fix it.

On 17 October Mandiant reported "zero-day exploitation of this vulnerability in the wild beginning in late August 2023", and that "the session takeovers bypassed password and multi-factor authentication". CISA added it to KEV on 18 October.

**The bug class.** After the fix shipped, researchers at Assetnote compared old and new firmware (patch diffing) and [published the cause](https://www.assetnote.io/resources/research/citrix-bleed-leaking-session-tokens-with-cve-2023-4966). A function built a small JSON reply with `snprintf` into a buffer of 0x20000 bytes (131,072), inserting the host name taken from the request's `Host` header. It then sent as many bytes as `snprintf` returned.

In C, `snprintf(buf, size, ...)` writes at most `size - 1` characters plus a terminating zero, and "returns how many bytes it would have written to the buffer if the buffer was big enough", not how many it did write. A long enough host name made the return value larger than the buffer, and the appliance sent the buffer plus the memory after it. The patch sends the reply only if the return value is less than 0x20000.

The model below shrinks the buffer to 40 bytes and places a fake session token right after it.

blocks.prompt: The normal reply is 36 bytes long and fits the 40-byte buffer. With a host name 20 characters longer, what will snprintf return, and what will the vulnerable code send?
blocks.reveal: `snprintf` returns 56, the length the full reply would have had. Only 39 characters and a zero fit in the buffer, but the code sends 56 bytes: the 40 buffer bytes and then the first 16 bytes of the neighbouring token, `sess=9F2C41A7E0B`. The fixed version sees 56 >= 40 and refuses to send anything.

blocks.caption: Compile with cc -Wall -Wextra bleed.c. Simplified model: real heap layouts differ, but the mistake is the same: trusting snprintf's return value as a length. Memory is one array here so the demo itself stays within bounds.

blocks.code:
# output (a zero byte is printed as a dot)
snprintf returned 36 (buffer holds 40)
{"issuer":"https://vpn.example.com"}
snprintf returned 56 (buffer holds 40)
{"issuer":"https://vpn.example.com.aaaa.sess=9F2C41A7E0B
snprintf returned 56 (buffer holds 40)
refused: too long

blocks.title: Sending n bytes from a 40-byte buffer (each cell is 4 bytes)

scenes.caption: Simplified memory: cells 0 to 9 are the 40-byte reply buffer. Cells 10 to 13 hold the start of another user's session token, which happens to be next.
Normal host name: snprintf writes 36 bytes plus a zero and returns 36. The code sends 36 bytes, cells 0 to 8. Correct, by luck of the length.
Long host name: the buffer fills (39 characters and a zero) and snprintf returns 56. The code sends 56 bytes: the whole buffer and 16 bytes of the token.
Fixed: compare the return value with the buffer size first. 56 >= 40, so nothing is sent. NetScaler's patch added exactly this comparison.

blocks.title: From leaked memory to a hijacked session

scenes.caption: Ana logs in with a password and an MFA code. NetScaler issues a session cookie and keeps it in memory.
The attacker sends unauthenticated requests with an over-long Host header. Some replies carry memory that includes a valid session cookie.
The attacker presents Ana's cookie. NetScaler treats the request as Ana's session: no password and no MFA are asked, because both already happened.
The admin patches. The leak stops, but the stolen session is still valid. Only killing all active and persistent sessions, as NetScaler advised, ends it.

blocks.md:
**Real impact.** CISA's joint advisory AA23-325A (21 November 2023) describes LockBit 3.0 affiliates using Citrix Bleed to get initial access to Boeing Distribution Inc., the parts and distribution business of Boeing, which shared what it saw. LockBit 3.0 is a ransomware family; "affiliates" are the criminal groups who break into victims and deploy it. With a hijacked session, the advisory says, actors "harvest credentials, move laterally, and access data and resources".

The same advisory asked organisations to patch internet-facing systems "within 24 to 48 hours of vulnerability disclosure", and, if compromise is suspected, to "assume that threat actors hold full administrative access".

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: install the fixed build, then kill all active and persistent sessions so stolen ones die with the old ones.
- *Detect*: hard. The appliance's web server did not log requests to the vulnerable endpoint, so Mandiant pointed to logs from WAFs or other devices in front of it. In NetScaler's `ns.log`, an SSL VPN session whose `Client_ip` (where the session began) differs from `Source` (where this connection comes from), or one address using several accounts within hours, deserves a look (lesson 10 turns this into code). Memory **core dumps** (a copy of a process's memory written to disk) of exploited appliances held human-readable strings over 120,000 characters long, more than 99% of them the character 0.
- *Respond*: treat every session and every credential used through the appliance during the exposure window as stolen; reset passwords and hunt on internal systems those users reached.

MFA protects the login, not the session. Anything that leaks or steals a session token after login bypasses MFA completely, which is why session lifetime, session binding and killing sessions after an incident matter.

blocks.question: snprintf(buf, 40, ...) returns 56. What does 56 mean?
options: 56 bytes were written into buf, overflowing it
It is an error code
The full output would have been 56 bytes; only 39 characters and a terminating zero were written
It is the address of the buffer
blocks.explain: snprintf truncates safely but reports the length it would have needed. Using that number as a send length is the bug; comparing it with the buffer size is the fix.

blocks.question: You installed the NetScaler fix on 11 October 2023, the day after it shipped. Why could an attacker still be using your gateway on 20 October?
options: The fix did not install
A session cookie stolen before the fix stayed valid until sessions were killed
The fix turned off MFA
NetScaler cannot be patched
blocks.explain: Exploitation began in late August. The fix stops new leaks but does not invalidate tokens already taken; NetScaler's guidance was to kill all active and persistent sessions after updating.

lessons.title: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker

blocks.md:
An **exploit chain** links bugs that are limited on their own. A bug that lets you skip login but only reach harmless pages, plus a bug that runs commands but only for logged-in administrators, together give command execution for anyone on the internet.

That is what hit Ivanti Connect Secure, the same SSL VPN product line as Pulse Connect Secure in lesson 3, under its new name. The tools used to check whether a device had been compromised turned out to be part of the story too.

**Discovery.** In the second week of December 2023, Volexity saw lateral movement (an intruder hopping between machines inside a network) at a customer whose network it monitored, and **webshells** on internal and external web servers (a webshell is a small script planted on a web server that runs the commands sent to it). The trail led to the customer's internet-facing Ivanti VPN, whose "logs had been wiped and logging had been disabled". Suspicious activity went back to 3 December.

From memory images of the appliance, Volexity recovered two zero-days: CVE-2023-46805, an authentication bypass (CVSS 8.2), and CVE-2024-21887, a command injection (CVSS 9.1). Volexity tracked the actor as UTA0178 and believed it to be a Chinese nation-state-level actor.

**The bug classes, at advisory level.** The analysis by Rapid7, a security company, found that the front-end web server decided whether a request needed login by comparing only the start of its path with a public endpoint (a C `strncmp` on the first characters). Anything after that prefix, including `..` segments, was passed on to an internal REST API (Representational State Transfer: an HTTP interface that programs call) meant for administrators. One of its endpoints placed a parameter into a shell command: command injection (recall *OS command injection: the shell is an interpreter too*).

It is lesson 3's mistake again: the security decision is made on the raw text, and the path is interpreted afterwards. The toy below uses made-up routes.

blocks.code:
import posixpath
PUBLIC = {"/api/public/help"}          # the only route open before login

def vulnerable(path):
    if path.startswith("/api/public/help"):   # prefix test on raw path
        return "no login, handled by " + posixpath.normpath(path)
    return "401 login required"

def fixed(path):
    route = posixpath.normpath(path)          # resolve first
    if route in PUBLIC:                       # then exact match
        return "no login, handled by " + route
    return "401 login required"

p = "/api/public/help/../../admin/run"
print(vulnerable(p))
print(fixed(p))

# output
no login, handled by /api/admin/run
401 login required
blocks.caption: Decide on the resolved route, by exact match, never on a prefix of the raw path. Real frameworks should also refuse paths that contain '..' after URL decoding.

blocks.title: The chain, as Volexity and Rapid7 described it

nodes.label:
Shell command built
from a parameter

Login page script
edited to copy passwords

RDP, SMB, SSH into
the network

scenes.caption: The front end lets any path that starts with a public endpoint through without login.
Because only the prefix was checked, '..' later in the path reached admin API endpoints without login: CVE-2023-46805, the authentication bypass.
One endpoint put a parameter into a shell command: CVE-2024-21887. Chained, anyone on the internet could run commands on the VPN.
Volexity saw the next steps: a backdoored CGI script, login page JavaScript changed to capture typed passwords, then those passwords used over RDP, SMB and SSH inside.

blocks.md:
**Timeline.** Ivanti disclosed both CVEs on 10 January 2024 with a temporary mitigation but no patch; CISA added them to KEV the same day. On 15 January Volexity reported evidence of compromise on "over 1,700 devices worldwide" and other actors joining in. CISA issued Emergency Directive 24-01 on 19 January (an emergency directive is an order US federal civilian agencies must follow, for urgent threats). The first patches came on 31 January and 1 February, and CISA's supplemental direction of 31 January ordered agencies to disconnect every Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure device by 2 February.

Volexity's warning from day one applies to every case in this course: "a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise".

**The integrity checker.** Ivanti shipped an **Integrity Checker Tool** (ICT): an internal version that runs periodically on the appliance, and an external version you download and run on demand. Both compare the files on the device with the vendor's list of known-good files and report changed or new ones. Volexity used it, but also found entries the attacker had added to the checker's exclusions list, "designed to evade the In-build Integrity Checker Tool". CISA's AA24-060B later described an attacker script that "creates a series of entries into files associated with the In-build Integrity Checker Tool to evade detection when periodic scans are run".

The toy checker below shows why that works. Its known-good hashes are fine; the problem is that it runs on the box, reading its skip list from the box.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

def h(data):
    return hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()[:12]

# Vendor's known-good manifest for this release: path to hash
manifest = {"/web/login.js": h(b"login page v22.3"),
            "/cgi/compcheck.cgi": h(b"compliance check v22.3")}

# What is on the appliance's disk after an intruder with root has been there
disk = {"/web/login.js": b"login page v22.3 + copy typed passwords out",
        "/cgi/compcheck.cgi": b"compliance check v22.3 + run ?cmd=",
        "/tmp/s.py": b"socks proxy"}

def check(skip):
    bad = [p for p, good in manifest.items()
           if p not in skip and h(disk.get(p, b"")) != good]
    new = [p for p in disk if p not in manifest and p not in skip
           and not p.startswith("/tmp/")]          # temp files ignored
    return bad, new

print("honest checker:  ", check(skip=set()))
# The checker runs ON the box and reads its exclusion list FROM the box.
# Root can add the changed files to that list.
print("after tampering: ", check(skip={"/web/login.js", "/cgi/compcheck.cgi"}))

# output
honest checker:   (['/web/login.js', '/cgi/compcheck.cgi'], [])
after tampering:  ([], [])
blocks.caption: Simplified model of an on-box integrity check. Ignoring /tmp is realistic for a checker; Volexity found the attacker ran tools from /tmp that were gone by the time of analysis.

blocks.title: The same check, before and after the skip list is edited
blocks.code:
def check(skip):
    bad = [p for p, good in manifest.items()
           if p not in skip and h(disk[p]) != good]
    new = [p for p in disk if p not in manifest
           and p not in skip and not p.startswith("/tmp/")]
    return bad, new

check(skip=set())
check(skip={"/web/login.js", "/cgi/compcheck.cgi"})

scenes.caption: Honest run: both changed files hash differently from the manifest, so both are reported.
The proxy script in /tmp is skipped by design, so 'new' stays empty even on the honest run.
With root, the intruder adds the two changed files to the skip list stored on the device.
Same code, same manifest: nothing is compared, and the report is clean on a backdoored appliance.

blocks.md:
CISA's advisory AA24-060B (29 February 2024) went further. In incident response it found that "Ivanti's internal and external Integrity Checker Tool (ICT)" missed compromises: webshells sat on devices with no file mismatches, and attackers had overwritten files, **time-stomped** them (reset file timestamps so changes look old) and remounted a partition "to return the appliance to a 'clean state'". In CISA's own lab, an attacker with these bugs could keep "root level persistence despite issuing factory resets and appliance upgrades". A **factory reset** restores the vendor's original software and settings; persistence that survives it is described as **rootkit**-level: malware that controls the system reporting on it, so the system cannot be trusted to report it.

The supplemental direction's verdict: assume "rootkit-level persistence that can survive a factory reset".

**Defender view and response.** To return a device to service, ED 24-01's supplemental direction required agencies to rebuild it per Ivanti's instructions and upgrade it, revoke and reissue every connected certificate, key and password, and reset local and service accounts. Because the VPN handled domain logins, agencies had to "assume domain accounts associated with the affected products have been compromised" and, by 1 March 2024, "reset passwords twice for on premise accounts, revoke Kerberos tickets", then revoke cloud tokens. Kerberos (named after the three-headed watchdog of Greek myth) is the Windows domain login protocol; its tickets stand in for a password for hours, so they must be revoked as well as the password changed.

AA24-060B adds: limit outbound internet connections from SSL VPN appliances, and keep hunting on systems the device touched. For the architectural answer (per-application access instead of one VPN gate), see the lesson *Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024* in the *Security architecture and zero trust* course.

A clean integrity check is evidence, not proof. If an attacker reached root, the checker ran on a system the attacker controls. Trust measurements taken from outside the device, and rebuild when root was possible.

blocks.question: Why did the toy on-box integrity checker report nothing on a backdoored appliance?
options: Its known-good hashes were wrong
SHA-256 is broken
It only checks files in /tmp
The intruder had root and edited the skip list the checker reads from the same device
blocks.explain: The manifest was correct. The checker trusted configuration stored on the device it was checking. Volexity found the real attacker adding entries to the ICT's files; CISA later found even the external ICT missed compromises.

blocks.question: On 10 January 2024 Ivanti published a mitigation, with patches still weeks away. Which of these did applying the mitigation NOT do?
options: Remove webshells, modified files and stolen passwords from devices already compromised
Block the known route to the vulnerable endpoints
Reduce exposure while waiting for patches
Buy time for a planned rebuild
blocks.explain: A mitigation stops new exploitation by the known path. It does nothing about what the attacker already changed or took, which is why Volexity said a mitigation does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise.

lessons.title: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command

blocks.md:
Some bugs are two harmless-looking steps far apart. Step one: anyone can create an empty file whose **name** they choose. Step two: a scheduled job, running as root, lists files in a folder and pastes their names into a shell command. Neither step looks like remote code execution. Together they are.

This was CVE-2024-3400 in GlobalProtect, the remote access VPN feature of PAN-OS, the operating system of Palo Alto Networks' firewalls. Recall from *Injection: when data becomes code*: a shell treats some characters (backticks, `$( )`, `;`) as instructions, so text pasted into a shell command can become code.

**Discovery.** On 10 April 2024 Volexity received alerts about "suspect network traffic emanating from the customer's firewall" and found the firewall had been compromised; it saw identical exploitation at a second customer the next day. It tracked the actor as UTA0218. The earliest evidence of attempted exploitation was 26 March 2024, when the attacker appeared to test the bug by "placing zero-byte files on firewall devices".

Palo Alto Networks published its advisory on 12 April: unauthenticated code execution "with root privileges on the firewall", for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.0 and 11.1 with a GlobalProtect gateway or portal configured, scored CVSS 10.0. Until fixes shipped, the interim mitigation was a Threat Prevention signature (a vendor-supplied intrusion prevention rule that blocks the attack traffic). CISA added it to KEV the same day. The fixed versions 10.2.9-h1, 11.0.4-h1 and 11.1.2-h3 shipped on 14 April, and Palo Alto declared all necessary fixes available on 15 April; courtesy hotfixes for older maintenance releases followed through 18 April.

**The bug, at advisory level.** Rapid7's analysis of the patch found that GlobalProtect stored data for unauthenticated sessions in a file named after the `SESSID` cookie, without checking the value. Path characters in the cookie let a request create an empty file with a chosen name in another folder, as root. A telemetry job run by cron (the Unix scheduler) later read file names from a folder and built a `curl` command string, run with `shell=True`, so the shell interpreted special characters in the file name.

The patch added a check that a session ID "is a valid UUID value" (a universally unique identifier: 32 hex digits in a fixed 8-4-4-4-12 pattern) before it names a file.

One more lesson in humility: the first advisory said only devices with telemetry enabled were exposed. watchTowr Labs, a security research firm, notes that Palo Alto later confirmed "telemetry is not required", and the advisory now says device telemetry "does not need to be enabled".

scenes.caption: The cookie value is used as part of a file name. With path characters in it, the file lands in a folder of the sender's choosing.
Later, the telemetry job lists that folder and builds a command string from the names it finds.
The string is run by a shell, which treats special characters in the file name as code. The commands run as root on the firewall.
Volexity saw configuration exported, then a firewall service account that was a domain admin used over SMB and WinRM to copy the Active Directory database.

blocks.caption: A toy version of the second step and both fixes. The harmless echo stands in for any command; run it in your own sandbox.

blocks.prompt: Before reading the output: the evil file name is day/x`echo INJECTED`. What will upload_vulnerable print, and what will upload_fixed print?
blocks.reveal: `upload_vulnerable` prints `uploading day/xINJECTED`: the shell ran `echo INJECTED` inside the backticks and pasted its output into the command. `upload_fixed` prints the name exactly as it is, backticks included, because no shell ever reads it; the name is one argument to the echo program.

# output
uploading day/stats-0412.json

uploading day/x`echo INJECTED`
True

blocks.caption: Two independent fixes: never pass a string through a shell (use an argument list), and validate untrusted values (a session ID must be a UUID) before they name files. Palo Alto's patch did both: a UUID check in GlobalProtect, and an argument list with shell=False in the telemetry script.

blocks.md:
**What the attacker did next** (Volexity): a cron job that fetched and ran a remote script every minute; a copy of the running configuration placed in a web folder for download; tunnelling tools; and, in one victim, "a service account configured for use by the Palo Alto firewall, and a member of the domain admins group" used to pivot inside via SMB and WinRM (Windows Remote Management, a protocol for running commands on Windows machines remotely). The targets were the domain's backup DPAPI keys (Windows Data Protection API keys, which protect saved secrets) and NTDS.dit, the Active Directory database holding every account's password hash. Volexity: the stolen data "did allow the attacker to effectively compromise credentials for all domain accounts".

A firewall does not need domain admin rights. Give its service account the least it needs.

**Defender view.**

- *Detect*: Palo Alto's advisory gives a check of the GlobalProtect log, `gpsvc.log`, for "failed to unmarshal session(...)" entries. A normal value there looks like a GUID (Microsoft's name for a UUID); a file path or shell characters means an attempted exploit. Volexity's first signal was network: alerts on suspect traffic leaving the firewall itself. Its examples include direct-to-IP `wget` downloads from the firewall, which it had not seen "outside of the attacker activity".
- *Respond*: collect a tech support file (TSF, the vendor's diagnostic bundle) before rebooting into a fixed version, because the advisory warns that some logs from the prior installation then "become inaccessible" on the device. From 3 May 2024 Palo Alto offered an Enhanced Factory Reset, after third parties showed post-exploit persistence techniques that "survive resets and upgrades".
- *Prevent*: patch, restrict outbound traffic from the firewall's own address, and remove domain admin rights from appliance service accounts.

Early interim guidance can be wrong. The first CVE-2024-3400 advisory tied exposure to telemetry; that was later corrected. Use a vendor workaround to buy hours, then install the fix and verify, rather than treating the workaround as the answer.

blocks.question: Which single change would have stopped the first step of CVE-2024-3400, file creation from the cookie?
options: Disabling the web console
Running the telemetry job less often
Checking that the session ID is a valid UUID before using it in a file name
Using HTTPS instead of HTTP
blocks.explain: The first step needed path characters in the cookie to end up in a file name. A strict UUID check rejects them; that is the check Palo Alto's patch added. The shell=True fix stops the second step.

blocks.question: Why should you collect a tech support file from a suspected PAN-OS victim before upgrading to the fixed version?
options: The upgrade will not install without one
After the reboot into the new version, some logs from the prior installation become inaccessible on the device
It speeds up the upgrade
It deletes the attacker's files
blocks.explain: Evidence first, then the fix. Upgrading changes the system you need to examine; the advisory's FAQ says exactly this, and BOD 26-04's forensic triage steps (lesson 11) put collection before patching for the same reason.

lessons.title: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously

blocks.md:
Last week your outside-in scan showed three VPN and firewall addresses. This week it shows four. The fourth answers on port 443 with a NetScaler Gateway login page, and nobody in the network team recognises the address. Is it yours? Is it patched? Who can turn it off?

Recall from *Penetration testing methodology and recon* (lesson *Attack surface management: recon as a defender*): **attack surface management** discovers what you expose to the internet and diffs it on a schedule. **Exposure management** builds on it: for each exposed thing, decide whether it matters right now (is it an edge product with exploited bugs, is it past its support date, is it a management interface?), get it fixed by a named owner, and check that the fix holds.

The US federal government now writes this into its patch directive. BOD 26-04 (Binding Operational Directive 26-04, 10 June 2026; a binding operational directive is an order US federal civilian agencies must follow) requires agencies to "continuously identify and tag all agency-owned assets that can be reached from outside the agency network and using a routable IP address". Each tag records organisation, environment (production or development), exposure (public or internal) and asset type (server, application or network device). Exposure matters because, as lesson 8 shows, it changes the deadline.

The same directive defines **publicly exposed** as "accessible to unauthenticated or untrusted entities via public networks, such as the internet, regardless of its physical or logical location". A cloud VM and a box in your server room are judged the same way.

nodes.label:
Match to inventory:
owner, product, version

Enrich: KEV, vendor
advisories, support date

Fix or mitigate:
patch, block, retire

scenes.caption: Start from what the internet sees, not from what the inventory says. The outside view finds the NetScaler nobody listed.
Every exposed address needs an owner. An address with no owner is a finding on its own, before any vulnerability is known.
Enrichment joins in what attackers already know: KEV entries and vendor advisories for that product, and whether it is past end of support.
Rank by exposure and evidence of exploitation first, then fix through the owner, then rescan to prove the change. Then do it again next cycle.

blocks.md:
**Where the outside view comes from.**

- *Your own scans* from an external host, using the Nmap skills from the prerequisite course.
- *Internet-wide search engines.* [Shodan](https://help.shodan.io/the-basics/what-is-shodan) describes itself as "a search engine for Internet-connected devices": it connects to every address it can and stores the **banners** (the text a service sends describing itself, such as a server name and version). One listed use: "keep an eye on all devices at your company that are facing the Internet".
- *Free notification services.* The [Shadowserver Foundation](https://www.shadowserver.org/what-we-do/network-reporting/) sends free daily reports built from "daily Internet-wide scans, sinkholes, honeypot sensors" to more than 10,000 subscribers, covering exposed and vulnerable services on the networks they own.

Banners lie both ways (recall backporting from the prerequisite), so an outside match is a lead to confirm through the owner, not a verdict.

blocks.code:
# What an outside-in scan found this week: (address, port, product seen)
scan = [
    ("203.0.113.10", 443,  "Ivanti Connect Secure"),
    ("203.0.113.11", 443,  "FortiOS SSL VPN"),
    ("203.0.113.40", 443,  "NetScaler Gateway"),
    ("198.51.100.7", 443,  "nginx"),
]
# What the asset inventory (CMDB) says we own, with an owner per address
inventory = {"203.0.113.10": "netops", "203.0.113.11": "netops",
             "198.51.100.7": "web team"}
# Product lines on our KEV watch list (the counts from lesson 1)
watch = ("Connect Secure", "FortiOS", "NetScaler", "PAN-OS", "BIG-IP",
         "SonicOS", "SMA", "Adaptive Security")

for ip, port, product in scan:
    owner = inventory.get(ip)
    flags = []
    if owner is None:
        flags.append("UNKNOWN ASSET: find an owner")
    if any(w in product for w in watch):
        flags.append("edge product: patch within days, hunt")
    print(f"{ip:13} {port} {product:22} {owner or '?':9} {'; '.join(flags)}")

# output
203.0.113.10  443 Ivanti Connect Secure  netops    edge product: patch within days, hunt
203.0.113.11  443 FortiOS SSL VPN        netops    edge product: patch within days, hunt
203.0.113.40  443 NetScaler Gateway      ?         UNKNOWN ASSET: find an owner; edge product: patch within days, hunt
198.51.100.7  443 nginx                  web team
blocks.caption: Toy data with documentation addresses. A real version reads scan exports and the CMDB (configuration management database, the inventory of IT assets) and opens tickets instead of printing.

blocks.md:
**A KEV watch list for edge products.** Lesson 1's script found seven edge product lines with 105 KEV entries between them. Turn that into a standing rule: when a new KEV entry, vendor advisory or emergency directive names a product line you run at the edge, the clock starts at once, not at the next monthly patch meeting. CCCS's edge device guidance lists the basics: subscribe to security notifications from each device's vendor, and "maintain an inventory of edge devices and their respective support timelines". CISA offers email alerts for KEV additions, and the KEV JSON feed can be polled by a script.

The NetScaler in the example matters twice: it is unowned, and it is a product line with 21 KEV entries. Unowned devices are the ones nobody patches, and nobody is watching their logs either.

KEV lists only what is already exploited. For edge CVEs not yet in it, EPSS (recall from *Security from zero*: the probability a CVE is exploited in the next 30 days) is an early warning: a rising score on a product you expose starts the clock early.

Exposure management is attack surface discovery plus judgement plus follow-through: see what the internet sees, tie each item to an owner and to what attackers are exploiting, and verify every fix from the outside.

blocks.question: Your external scan finds a NetScaler Gateway on an address that is not in the inventory. What should happen first?
options: Ignore it until a vulnerability scanner flags a CVE
Treat it as a finding now: find the owner, confirm the version and support status, and block it if no owner appears
Run an exploit against it to prove it is vulnerable
Delete it from the scan results
blocks.explain: An unowned internet-facing edge product is a risk before any CVE is known: nobody patches it or reads its logs. Testing it with an exploit is out of bounds unless you own it and have authorisation; ownership comes first.

blocks.question: Why combine an outside-in scan with the asset inventory instead of trusting either one alone?
options: The scan finds what is really exposed, including unknown devices; the inventory supplies owners and true versions. Each corrects the other
Scans are always more accurate than inventories
Inventories are required by law, scans are not
It makes the scan faster
blocks.explain: Equifax's scans missed a vulnerable system (prerequisite course), and inventories miss devices people set up without telling anyone. The join of the two is what produces actionable, owned findings.

lessons.title: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices

blocks.md:
How long do you have between a patch and attacks? Mandiant measures **time to exploit** (TTE), "the average time taken to exploit a vulnerability before or after a patch is released": days from the patch to first exploitation, negative when exploitation came first. Its 2024 analysis of 2023 found: "Through 2018 to 2019, we observed an average TTE of 63 days. From 2020 to the start of 2021, that number decreased to 44 days... across all of 2021 and 2022... 32 days... In 2023... an average of just five days." Of 138 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2023 and exploited, 97 were zero-days.

M-Trends 2026 reports that "the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities dropped to an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation is routinely occurring before a patch is even released".

blocks.title: Mandiant's average time to exploit, in days

scenes.caption: Each bar is the average time from a patch's release to first exploitation in that period. A 30-day patch cycle was once inside the window.
By 2023 the average was five days. M-Trends 2026 puts the 2025 estimate below zero (-7 days, not drawn): on average, exploitation now starts before the fix.

blocks.md: The four cases with clear dates show the same thing at the edge. In the timeline, every lane is shifted so that the day its fix shipped falls on day 60.

blocks.title: Exploitation before and after the fix (fix shipped on day 60)

scenes.caption: Ivanti: suspicious activity from 3 December 2023, 59 days before the first patches on 31 January. For the last 21 days only a mitigation existed.
Citrix Bleed: Mandiant found zero-day use from late August 2023, about six weeks before the 10 October fix (start shown approximately).
PAN-OS: first test exploitation on 26 March 2024, 20 days before Palo Alto declared all necessary fixes available on 15 April.
Pulse 2019 was the older pattern, an n-day: fixed on 24 April 2019, with 14,500 servers still unpatched 122 days later, and exploitation running on for months.

blocks.md:
So a deadline for edge devices has two jobs: patch fast, and check whether you were already hit. BOD 26-04 builds both into one table. It asks four questions per vulnerable asset:

1. Is the asset **publicly exposed**? (Yours to answer, from lesson 7.)
2. Is the CVE in **KEV**?
3. Is it **automatable**: can an attacker automate every step of exploitation?
4. Is the **technical impact** partial or total control? (Total includes an exploit that "reliably reveals log-in credentials".)

The last two come from **SSVC** (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization), a [decision-tree method](https://certcc.github.io/SSVC/) published by the CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC) at Carnegie Mellon University. CISA publishes the answers for every CVE through its **Vulnrichment** programme, as an Authorized Data Publisher (ADP) block inside each CVE record. The table turns the four answers into calendar days: 3 days and forensic triage, 3, 14, 60, or fix on the next upgrade. The clock starts when CISA adds the CVE to KEV or when you detect it, whichever comes first.

blocks.code:
# BOD 26-04 Table 1 (CISA, 10 June 2026): calendar days to remediate.
# Key: (publicly exposed, in KEV, automatable, total control)
F, D3, D14, D60, UP = "3 days + forensic triage", "3 days", "14 days", "60 days", "next upgrade"
TABLE = {(1,1,1,1): F,  (1,1,1,0): D3,  (1,1,0,1): F,   (1,1,0,0): D14,

         (0,0,1,1): D60,(0,0,1,0): D60, (0,0,0,1): UP,  (0,0,0,0): UP}

         ("CVE-2023-4966  NetScaler",     1, 1),
         ("CVE-2023-46805 Ivanti",        1, 0),
         ("CVE-2024-21887 Ivanti",        0, 1),
         ("CVE-2024-3400  PAN-OS",        1, 1)]
print(f"{'':30}{'on the internet':27}{'internal only'}")
for name, auto, total in cases:
    print(f"{name:30}{TABLE[(1,1,auto,total)]:27}{TABLE[(0,1,auto,total)]}")

CVE-2023-46805 Ivanti         3 days                     14 days
