blocks.md:
**Reading the result.** Every exposed edge case here gets 3 days. Four of the six also require **forensic triage**: a structured check of whether the asset was already compromised (lesson 11). Taking the device off the internet buys time only where the bug is not both automatable and total control: CVE-2018-13379 goes from 3 to 14 days, but Pulse, Citrix Bleed and PAN-OS stay at 3 days and triage even on an internal network.

Note one judgement call visible in the data: CISA rates the FortiOS file read as partial control even though it leaked passwords. Your own risk view can be stricter than the federal table.

KEV entries now also carry a field, "Forensic triage required per BOD 26-04". In the 13 November 2026 feed, 105 of 1,781 entries say Yes, all added since the directive took effect (the earliest on 25 June 2026). The six older CVEs in this course all say No there, so treat the table as a guide to how hard to check them, not as what the feed flags.

**Making 3 days possible for edge devices.** Decide before the emergency:

- *Pre-approved emergency changes* for VPNs and firewalls, with a named owner who can approve downtime at night.
- *A standby or test device*: CCCS advises installing patches "after testing for reliability on a standby or test device", then swapping.
- *Rehearsed mitigations*: know how to turn off the vulnerable feature. Fortinet's only workaround in 2019 was disabling the SSL VPN; in 2025 Cisco advised disabling SSL VPN web services on affected firewalls.
- *Triage kit*: how to collect logs, a tech support file or a core dump for each product you run (lessons 10 and 11).

Mitigation is not remediation, and patching is not the end. For a KEV edge bug that is automatable or gives total control, assume exploitation may have come first: patch within days, then look for signs it already happened.

blocks.question: Under BOD 26-04, moving a FortiOS device with CVE-2018-13379 off the internet changes its deadline from 3 to 14 days. Why does Citrix Bleed stay at 3 days and forensic triage when internal?
options: Citrix Bleed is older
Internal assets are never exempt
CISA rates Citrix Bleed automatable with total control, and that row (row 9) stays at 3 days and triage even when not exposed
Because NetScaler is a load balancer
blocks.explain: The table keeps the strictest deadline for exploited bugs that are automatable and give total control, whatever the exposure. The FortiOS read is rated partial control, so its internal row is 14 days.

blocks.question: M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean time to exploit of -7 days. What does the negative sign mean for an edge patch process?
options: Patches arrive a week before bugs are found
On average, exploitation begins before a fix exists, so fast patching must be paired with checking for compromise that happened earlier
Attackers stopped using n-days
Vendors publish advisories a week late on purpose
blocks.explain: Negative TTE means exploitation precedes the patch. Speed still matters (it stops mass exploitation after disclosure), but forensic triage is what deals with the earlier window.

lessons.title: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet

blocks.md:
A firewall has two kinds of doors. The **data plane** carries the traffic it exists for: the VPN portal must answer the internet, or nobody can work from home. The **management plane** is how administrators run the device: a web admin page, SSH, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol, used to monitor and configure network devices). Tiny example: the VPN portal on port 443 of an address is necessary; the admin page on port 8443 of the same address is not.

A management interface reachable from the internet gives attackers a second, more powerful target, and its bugs often lead straight to administrator control.

CISA's **BOD 23-02**, "Mitigating the Risk from Internet-Exposed Management Interfaces" (13 June 2023), explains why: "Most device management interfaces are designed to be accessed from dedicated physical interfaces and/or management networks and are not meant to be accessible directly from the public internet."

It applies to routers, switches, firewalls, VPN concentrators, proxies, load balancers and "out of band server management interfaces (such as iLo and iDRAC)": the separate management controllers built into HPE servers (iLO, Integrated Lights-Out) and Dell servers (iDRAC, integrated Dell Remote Access Controller), which can power a server on and off and reinstall it. The protocols listed include HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SNMP, Telnet, TFTP, RDP, rlogin, RSH, SSH, SMB, VNC and X11. Cloud providers' own management portals and APIs are out of scope.

**What the directive requires.** Within 14 days of CISA notifying an agency, or the agency discovering an in-scope interface, it must do at least one of two things:

1. Remove the interface from the internet so it is reachable only from an internal network ("CISA recommends an isolated management network"), or
2. Put it behind "a policy enforcement point separate from the interface itself", as part of a zero trust architecture. CISA marks this as the "preferred action".

Agencies must also make sure new devices get one of these protections. CISA scans for exposed interfaces itself and notifies agencies, which is the outside-in view of lesson 7, run by someone else.

nodes.label:
Appliance: VPN portal
(must face the internet)

scenes.caption: Out of scope of BOD 23-02's fix: the VPN portal must be public. In scope: the admin page answers the same internet on the same address.
Option 1: the admin interface listens only on an isolated management network, reached from hardened admin workstations. The internet path is gone.
Option 2 (preferred by CISA): every admin connection must pass a separate policy enforcement point that checks identity and device before it reaches the interface.

blocks.md:
A **PAW** (privileged access workstation) is a hardened computer used only for administration, never for email or browsing. CCCS recommends that administrators do all security and configuration work from one, over "an out-of-band management network or administrative workstation that is physically separated from the operational data flow network".

CCCS also gives the case for this: a zero-day in a device's web configuration interface let attackers gain administrator access, create an account with a password they chose and plant files for persistence; its recommendation is that "network management interfaces (NMIs) should not be directly exposed to the Internet". The UK NCSC makes a related point about Ivanti: many exploited flaws "haven't been in the core service but in additional services (such as web portals and management interfaces)", so turn off or block every interface or portal you do not need.

blocks.caption: A compensating control in the style of the prerequisite's firewall lesson. Addresses are documentation examples. Verify with an outside scan that TCP 22 and 8443 now show as filtered (UDP 161 shows as open|filtered, since Nmap cannot tell a dropped UDP probe from a silent open port).

blocks.md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

blocks.question: Which setup meets BOD 23-02 for a firewall's web admin page?
options: The admin page stays on the internet with a long password
The admin page is moved to port 18443 so scanners miss it
The admin page is public but logs every login
The admin page answers only on an isolated management network reached from admin workstations
blocks.explain: BOD 23-02 accepts two options: remove the interface from the internet, or put a separate policy enforcement point in front of it. A strong password, an unusual port or logging leave the interface itself reachable.

blocks.question: Does BOD 23-02 require an agency to take its public VPN portal off the internet?
options: Yes, all VPN services must be internal
No. It covers management interfaces; the VPN service itself may stay public (other rules, such as patch deadlines, still apply to it)
Yes, unless the portal sits behind a separate policy enforcement point
No, because VPN portals count as cloud management interfaces, which are out of scope
blocks.explain: The directive defines a networked management interface as one meant exclusively for administrators. The user-facing VPN service is the device's job, so it is not in scope, although BOD 26-04 still sets its patch deadlines.

lessons.title: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside

blocks.md:
You cannot install EDR on most appliances, and an intruder with root can wipe or fake the logs stored on them. So defenders watch **around** the device: what it sends to the network, what its forwarded logs say about sessions, and what the accounts that pass through it do inside.

Tiny example: a VPN appliance has talked to the same few addresses for a year (the vendor's update server, your log collector, your directory). One night it opens a connection to an unknown address and downloads a file. No log on the appliance needs to survive for you to see that, as long as a firewall or network sensor next to it records the connection.

**Signals from this course's cases.**

- *Outbound traffic from the appliance itself.* Ivanti: `curl` to an IP geolocation service and to 1.1.1.1, reverse SOCKS proxies (relays for the attacker's traffic) and SSH tunnels (Volexity). PAN-OS: direct-to-IP `wget` downloads from the firewall. AA24-060B's advice follows: limit outbound internet connections from SSL VPN appliances to what they need.
- *Session anomalies.* NetScaler: a session whose `Client_ip` differs from the `Source` of a later connection, or one address using many accounts within hours (Mandiant).
- *Logins through the device from odd places.* Pulse: stolen passwords used from Tor and rented servers (CISA). Ivanti: VPN users' credentials used over RDP, SMB and SSH from unusual internal hosts.
- *Log oddities.* Logs wiped or logging disabled (Ivanti); `gpsvc.log` session IDs that are paths, not GUIDs (PAN-OS); unauthenticated requests containing traversal sequences (Pulse).
- *Changes.* New admin accounts, configuration changes, firmware changes outside a change window (CCCS: alert on all of these).
Mandiant's two NetScaler hunts translate into a few lines of code. The log lines below are shaped like NetScaler's SSL VPN `TCPCONNSTAT` events, with made-up values; real lines carry more fields.

blocks.code:
import re
from collections import defaultdict

# Lines shaped like NetScaler SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT events (values made up)
log = """\
2023-10-20 08:01 SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT - User ana - Client_ip 198.51.100.20 - Source 198.51.100.20
2023-10-20 08:05 SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT - User raj - Client_ip 203.0.113.77 - Source 203.0.113.77
2023-10-20 09:12 SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT - User ana - Client_ip 198.51.100.20 - Source 192.0.2.66
2023-10-20 09:14 SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT - User raj - Client_ip 203.0.113.77 - Source 192.0.2.66
2023-10-20 09:20 SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT - User lee - Client_ip 192.0.2.66 - Source 192.0.2.66"""

pat = re.compile(r"User (\S+) - Client_ip (\S+) - Source (\S+)")
users_by_source = defaultdict(set)
for line in log.splitlines():
    user, client, source = pat.search(line).groups()
    users_by_source[source].add(user)
    if client != source:                       # session used from elsewhere
        print("MISMATCH", line[:16], user, "from", client, "now", source)

for source, users in users_by_source.items():
    if len(users) >= 3:                        # one address, many accounts
        print("MANY USERS", source, sorted(users))
blocks.caption: Both rules come from Mandiant's Citrix Bleed investigation. Both have innocent causes too: users change networks, and many staff can share one office address behind NAT.

blocks.title: Hunting hijacked sessions in forwarded NetScaler logs

scenes.caption: 08:01, ana: the session began at 198.51.100.20 and this connection comes from the same address. Nothing to report.
09:12, ana again: same session, but the connection now comes from 192.0.2.66. A session moving to a new address is what a stolen cookie looks like.
09:14, raj: that session also appears from 192.0.2.66. Two people's sessions, one stranger's address.
After all lines: 192.0.2.66 used three accounts within 8 minutes. Mandiant saw exactly this, attackers trying several accounts from one address within hours.

blocks.md:
**Getting the logs out, properly.** The NCSC forensic guidance sets the bar: forward logs in near real time with a standard protocol "protected using transport layer security (TLS)", stamp them in UTC with milliseconds, alert loudly when time synchronisation (NTP, the Network Time Protocol) fails, and warn administrators "if remote logging is disabled or misconfigured". M-Trends 2026 adds retention: keep network device logs in long-term central storage, because 90 days does not cover intrusions that last a year.

**Watching from the network.** Volexity found both the Ivanti and the PAN-OS intrusions through network security monitoring, not appliance logs. CISA noted that an IDS (intrusion detection system) able to see the VPN's external interface "may have noticed the exploitation" of the Pulse bug.

When you cannot see inside a device, watch its edges: every connection it starts, every session that changes address, every account that uses it, and every configuration change. Those records live on other systems the intruder does not control.

blocks.question: Which single signal is the strongest sign that an edge appliance itself is compromised?
options: A failed VPN login from a user who mistyped a password
The appliance starting a direct-to-IP download from an address it has never contacted
High CPU during business hours
A user connecting from home
blocks.explain: Appliances have short, predictable lists of destinations. Suspect traffic from the firewall itself was Volexity's first signal in the PAN-OS case, and direct-to-IP downloads from the device were a pattern it saw only from the attacker. The other options are everyday events.

blocks.question: Why enforce an outbound allowlist on the firewall in front of a VPN appliance, rather than relying on the appliance's own settings?
options: Appliance settings cannot be changed
It makes the VPN faster
If the appliance is taken over, its own settings are under the attacker's control; a separate device keeps blocking and logging
Allowlists are required by TLS
blocks.explain: A control on the compromised box can be switched off by the intruder. A separate enforcement and logging point keeps working, and its blocked-connection logs become detection signals. This is AA24-060B's advice.

lessons.title: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate

blocks.md:
Your VPN vendor has published a KEV-listed zero-day and you run the product. Patching right away feels responsible, but patching first can destroy the evidence of whether you were already compromised, and does not remove an intruder who got in earlier.

Order matters. BOD 26-04's implementation guidance sets out **forensic triage** in six steps with target times from the KEV addition. Its advice: "Do not alter or remediate systems prior to evidence/artifact collection when possible", and "Collect all required evidence prior to this step as patching may jeopardize the availability of artifacts".

blocks.title: BOD 26-04 forensic triage: target hours after a KEV addition

scenes.caption: Hours 0 to 2: decide whether the CVE requires triage, find every affected device, activate the team and set up an out-of-band channel that does not rely on possibly compromised systems.
Hours 2 to 24: collect volatile data first (memory, running state), then logs and disk. Patching happens in the same window, but only after collection.
Hours 6 to 24: contain. Isolate affected devices and the systems they reach, as soon as initial collection is done.
Hours 24 to 72: analyse for unauthorised access, persistence, lateral movement and data theft; then write the triage report and decide whether to escalate to full incident response.

blocks.md:
**Evidence from an appliance** is product-specific, so prepare the procedure for each product you run before you need it:

- *NetScaler*: Mandiant found exploitation traces in memory **core dumps** of the NSPPE process (NetScaler Packet Processing Engine, the process that handles the appliance's traffic), and warned "not to reboot the appliance prior to generating a core dump".
- *Cisco firewalls* (the ASA, Adaptive Security Appliance, line and its successors): CISA's Emergency Directive 25-03 (September 2025) had agencies follow its "Core Dump and Hunt Instructions" and, if compromise was found, "disconnect the device from their network (but do not power off)". Power off and the memory is gone.
- *PAN-OS*: collect the tech support file before rebooting into a fixed version.
- *Ivanti*: Volexity found the exploit chain itself in a memory image of the appliance.

Disconnect, do not switch off: isolation stops the damage while keeping memory for analysis.

**Rebuild, do not just patch.** CISA's revised version of ED 25-03 (V1) states that applying Cisco's security updates "does not necessarily remove an existing threat actor from the compromised device". In April 2026 Cisco reported that the actor behind a campaign it calls ArcaneDoor had persistence "preserved across upgrading to the fixed releases". Earlier, on older ASA 5500-X firewalls, Cisco had found the actor modifying ROMMON, part of the device's boot code, "to allow for persistence across reboots and software upgrades". Those models predate **Secure Boot** (each boot stage checks a signature before running the next); Cisco saw no such change on models with Secure Boot and Trust Anchor support.

The directive's remedy included a hard reset "by physically unplugging the device's power supply, as a reboot is not sufficient to expunge the malware". Cisco's advice after a suspected compromise: consider all configuration untrusted, reset to factory defaults after upgrading, and reconfigure from scratch "with new passwords, and re-generated certificates and keys".

blocks.code:
# runbook/edge-compromise.yaml : one page per edge product, written in advance
device: vpn-hq (Ivanti Connect Secure)
trigger: KEV entry or vendor advisory naming this product, or a detection
steps:
  - preserve: vendor snapshot or integrity tool output, memory image,
              forwarded logs for the whole exposure window (from the SIEM)
  - patch: fixed version or vendor mitigation, only after collection
  - isolate: block traffic at the upstream firewall; keep power ON
             (at once, before collection, if compromise is confirmed)
  - decide: keep and monitor only if triage finds no compromise;
            otherwise rebuild from vendor media on a fixed version
  - rotate:
      - local admin accounts and API keys on the device
      - LDAP bind / service accounts it uses (check their group rights)
      - portal TLS certificate and private key
      - passwords of every user who logged in during the window
      - kill sessions; revoke Kerberos tickets and cloud tokens
  - hunt: internal hosts reached via VPN sessions or the service accounts
  - report: triage report within 72 h; escalate if compromise confirmed
owner: netops on-call (approves downtime 24x7)
blocks.caption: A made-up runbook in YAML. The point is that it exists before the emergency, names an owner who can approve downtime, and lists the secrets to rotate for this specific device.

blocks.md: Evidence first, then the fix. Collect what the vendor's procedure allows before patching or rebooting, isolate without powering off once compromise is found, patch, and if compromise is possible rebuild and rotate every secret the device held or saw.

blocks.question: A Cisco firewall's core dump analysis returns 'Compromise Detected'. Under ED 25-03, what should you do with the device first?
options: Disconnect it from the network but keep it powered on, report it and work on eviction
Reboot it to clear the malware
Install the patch and put it back in service
Power it off immediately
blocks.explain: Disconnecting stops the intruder using it; keeping power preserves memory for analysis. A reboot does not remove this malware (the directive later required a full power removal as part of remediation, after evidence collection).

blocks.question: After a confirmed PAN-OS compromise, which item is most often forgotten in rotation?
options: The firewall's local admin password
The firewall's directory service account, which in Volexity's case was a domain admin
The firewall's hostname
The firewall's public IP address
blocks.explain: Admins remember the local admin password, but service accounts configured on appliances are easy to overlook because no person logs in with them. Volexity saw exactly such an account used to reach the domain controllers. Hostnames and addresses are not secrets.

lessons.title: End of support, hardening and the replace decision

blocks.md:
Every device has a date after which its vendor stops fixing it: **end of support** (EOS, also called end of life). Before that date a new bug is a race; after it, the bug stays open forever. On the edge, that means an internet-facing device that will collect KEV entries it can never fix.

BOD 26-02, "Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices" (5 February 2026), defines EOS as devices, firmware and software versions "that no longer receive timely, supported updates from the original equipment manufacturer", and explains why edge devices get their own directive: they are "attractive targets due to their extensive reach into an organization's network and integrations with identity management systems". It also says plainly that "EOS devices should not reside anywhere on federal networks".

blocks.title: BOD 26-02 deadlines, in months after 5 February 2026

scenes.caption: Immediately: any edge device still supported by its vendor but running EOS software must be updated to a supported version.
Within 3 months: inventory every device on CISA's EOS Edge Device List (product, version, support date) and report it to CISA.
Within 12 months: decommission listed devices whose EOS date falls by then, and inventory all edge devices going EOS in the following year. Within 18: decommission all identified EOS edge devices.
Within 24 months: a standing process to discover every edge device continuously and retire each one on or before its EOS date. The directive becomes a habit.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date

ISSUED = date(2026, 2, 5)                      # BOD 26-02
def months_after(d, m):
    y, mo = divmod(d.month - 1 + m, 12)
    return date(d.year + y, mo + 1, d.day)

for m, task in [(3, "inventory devices on CISA's EOS list"),
                (12, "remove listed devices EOS by then"),
                (18, "remove all identified EOS edge devices"),
                (24, "continuous discovery; replace before EOS")]:
    print(months_after(ISSUED, m), task)

today = date(2026, 11, 14)
fleet = [("vpn-hq",   "ASA 5545-X",   date(2025, 9, 30)),
         ("fw-branch","ASA 5516-X",   date(2026, 8, 31)),
         ("fw-dc",    "Firewall X",   date(2029, 6, 30))]
for name, model, eos in fleet:
    days = (eos - today).days
    state = "PAST EOS: replace now" if days < 0 else (
            "EOS within 12 months: plan" if days <= 365 else "supported")
    print(f"{name:10} {model:11} EOS {eos}  {days:5} days  {state}")

# output
2026-05-05 inventory devices on CISA's EOS list
2027-02-05 remove listed devices EOS by then
2027-08-05 remove all identified EOS edge devices
2028-02-05 continuous discovery; replace before EOS
vpn-hq     ASA 5545-X  EOS 2025-09-30   -410 days  PAST EOS: replace now
fw-branch  ASA 5516-X  EOS 2026-08-31    -75 days  PAST EOS: replace now
fw-dc      Firewall X  EOS 2029-06-30    959 days  supported
blocks.caption: Support dates for the two ASA models are Cisco's published last dates of support; 'Firewall X' is a made-up supported model. Run your own inventory through the same check monthly.

blocks.md:
**Why EOS edge devices are hunted.** CISA's Volt Typhoon advisory (AA24-038A) reports the group "used Cisco and NETGEAR end-of-life SOHO routers implanted with KV Botnet malware" to hide its traffic (SOHO: small office, home office). [Black Lotus Labs](https://blog.lumen.com/routers-roasting-on-an-open-firewall-the-kv-botnet-investigation/), the threat research team of the US network operator Lumen, investigated the botnet and found that its KV cluster "primarily consists of end-of-life products", and noted the "large supply of vastly out-of-date and generally considered end-of-life edge devices on the internet, no longer eligible to receive patches".

ArcaneDoor shows the same at enterprise scale. Cisco found ROMMON persistence only on ASA 5500-X models without Secure Boot, three of which reached their last date of support on 30 September 2025. ED 25-03 ordered agencies to "permanently disconnect" ASA models with support ending on or before that date by that same day: "these legacy platforms/releases cannot meet current vendor support and update requirements".

**When even a supported device must go.** In May 2023 Barracuda found that its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances had been exploited through CVE-2023-2868, with attacks dating back to October 2022. It pushed a patch on 20 May. On 6 June it told customers, as reported by [KrebsOnSecurity](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2023/06/barracuda-urges-replacing-not-patching-its-email-security-gateways/), that "impacted ESG appliances must be immediately replaced regardless of patch version level", and offered replacements at no cost. When the vendor cannot be sure its own update removes an intruder, the hardware itself is the problem.

**The replace-or-keep decision.** Ask of each edge device:

1. Is it supported, and will it be for the next year?
2. Does it support Secure Boot or equivalent, so persistence below the operating system is hard?
3. Can you get its logs out in real time, and collect memory and disk for an investigation (the NCSC forensic baseline)?
4. Can the vendor give evidence its product is secure by design? The NCSC's advice: "Where vendors can't provide evidence their product is secure by design, don't allow it on your perimeter", and consider a cloud-hosted service instead.
5. Does it need to be on the internet at all?
6. For a VPN bought now, does the vendor support or plan hybrid post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM)? NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange after 2030, well inside an appliance's service life.

A device that fails questions 1 or 2 is a replacement project with a date, not a patching task.

**Practice, legally.** The bug classes in this course have free labs at PortSwigger's Web Security Academy: [path traversal](https://portswigger.net/web-security/file-path-traversal) and [OS command injection](https://portswigger.net/web-security/os-command-injection). For log analysis and incident response, try [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/). For your own organisation, run the KEV script from lesson 1 against your inventory, and if you are responsible for a network, sign it up for Shadowserver's free reports.

A device that can no longer be patched, or that you cannot trust after a compromise, is not a vulnerability to manage: it is a replacement to schedule. Track support dates like expiry dates and replace before them.

blocks.question: An internet-facing firewall reached end of support last month. A new KEV entry covers its product line. What is the right plan?
options: Wait for the vendor's patch
Rely on the IPS signature forever
Lower its CVSS score in the scanner
Treat it as a replacement now: isolate or restrict it as a stop-gap, check it for compromise, and decommission it
blocks.explain: No patch will come after EOS. Stop-gaps (blocking exposure, signatures) buy time while it is replaced. BOD 26-02 sets the same direction for federal agencies, and ED 25-03 ordered EOS ASA models disconnected.

blocks.question: Barracuda asked customers to replace ESG appliances 'regardless of patch version level'. What does that tell a defender about patching?
options: Patches from Barracuda were never released
Once an appliance may hold persistence the vendor cannot reliably remove, patching cannot restore trust; only new hardware can
Email gateways cannot be patched
Replacement is always cheaper than patching
blocks.explain: The patch fixed the bug, but the vendor could not be confident that software updates removed the intruder from compromised devices. The same logic drives rebuilds for Ivanti and hard resets for Cisco.
